column6: The commentary hears 103:3 as a dying person's instruction passed to successors; Jacob, near death, asks Joseph to swear to carry out his burial request, making the bequest an explicit obligation.
Jacob specifies that he be carried from Egypt and buried with his fathers; this gives the commentary's otherwise implicit deathbed legacy a concrete patriarchal scene.
Joseph swears to do as Jacob asked, matching the commentary's joining of last instructions with an oath that binds the living after the speaker's death.

Dying Joseph tells his brothers that God will bring them from Egypt to the land promised their ancestors; like the commentary's counsel passed onward, his last words orient successors toward an inherited promise.
Joseph makes Israel's sons swear to carry his bones when God visits them; the oath preserves a charge and a physical trust across generations, beyond the speaker's life.
David announces that he is going the way of all the earth and addresses Solomon before dying; the scene supplies the explicit farewell frame implied by the commentary's image of counsel as a bequest.
David charges Solomon to keep God's commandments and walk in God's ways; this is a father's binding instruction to the successor who will carry his obligations forward.
The firstborn is owed a double portion as his right; this directly illuminates the commentary's claim that heirs' portions are rights rather than discretionary gifts.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew ḥ-q-q; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels بِٱلْحَقّ with Arabic root ḥ-q-q and calls heirs' shares rights; Numbers gives a succession rule for the nearest relative and calls it חֻקַּת מִשְׁפָּט, a prescribed judgment, showing how a cognate candidate's legal sense can secure inheritance.
The commentary calls the thing delivered an amanah; Exodus begins a case where money or goods are delivered to a neighbor for safekeeping and then stolen, giving that trust a concrete legal setting.
When no one saw what happened to a deposit, the law requires an oath between the parties; this closely joins the commentary's entrusted object and sworn witness in one legal procedure.

The law requires two or three witnesses to establish a matter; this is a specific legal counterpart to the commentary's two witnesses at a deathbed bequest, while setting a different evidentiary threshold.
Judges must investigate a malicious witness diligently; this adds a procedure for testing the oath-bound testimony that the commentary says can be challenged when fraud appears.
The false witness receives the penalty intended for the accused; alongside the commentary's replacement witnesses exposing fraud, this shows a different legal remedy for perjury.

The commentary's Arabic lexicon gloss for root ʿ-ṣ-r (B006) describes giving a gift and then withdrawing it; Psalm 15 praises the person who swears to their own hurt and does not change, a direct counter-image of retracting one's word.

The source commentary's dictionary gloss under Arabic root ʿ-ṣ-r (B006) is to give a gift and take it back; after Isaac realizes Jacob received the blessing, he says it will stand, portraying a paternal blessing as irretrievable rather than retracted.
Judah tells Jacob that he will be surety for Benjamin and accept blame if he fails to return him; this concretely matches the commentary's image of a guarantor standing behind another's obligation.
Judah says he became surety for the boy to his father and will bear blame if he does not bring him back; the repeated pledge makes the guarantor's personal liability explicit.

Those who fear God speak with one another, God listens, and a book of remembrance is written; the scene closely joins the commentary's mutual counsel with a record that preserves the speakers beyond the moment.

The speaker says the ancestors' deeds and praise of God will be told to the coming generation rather than hidden from their children; this makes the commentary's intergenerational handoff of truth a deliberate communal practice.
The command to speak truth each to his neighbor and render judgments of truth and peace gives a concrete communal form to the commentary's mutual enjoining of al-ḥaqq.

The letter commands each person to speak truth with their neighbor because they are members of one another; it closely matches the commentary's reciprocal counsel in truth and explains it through mutual belonging.
The community is told to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone; this gives specific practices for the commentary's mutual counsel and ṣabr.
Paul tells the Ephesian elders that they will see his face no more; this establishes the farewell setting for his entrusting them with teaching and inheritance in the next part of the speech.

As he departs, Paul commends the elders to God and the word of grace, which can build them up and give them an inheritance; this is a striking Christian scene of a departing teacher handing successors both a trust and an inheritance.
The writer tells Timothy to guard the good deposit entrusted to him; this makes the commentary's image of a delivered amanah into a specific charge to preserve teaching.

Timothy is to entrust what he heard before many witnesses to faithful people able to teach others; the four-stage chain concretely develops the commentary's counsel handed from one generation to another.
The readers are urged to imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promises; this uniquely combines the commentary's faith and ṣabr with its image of heirs receiving what is due.

The mediator's death is linked to the called receiving the promised eternal inheritance; Hebrews supplies a Christian interpretation in which death and inheritance belong together, as in the commentary's testament image.
Hebrews says a death is necessary for a testament to take effect; this makes explicit the legal logic behind the commentary's dying speaker leaving a binding word to survivors.
A testament is said to take effect only after the maker dies; this sharpens the commentary's metaphor of advice as a last bequest by explaining when such a bequest binds.
Paul writes in his own hand that he will repay what Onesimus owes; this is a direct Christian instance of the commentary's guarantor personally standing behind another's debt.
Hebrews recalls that Joseph, near death, gave instructions about his bones; it interprets the Genesis deathbed oath as an act of faith transmitted beyond the testator's life.

column5: Arabic ʾ-m-n / Hebrew ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels ءَامَنُوا۟ with Arabic root ʾ-m-n; Deuteronomy calls God הָאֵל הַנֶּאֱמָן, faithful and covenant-keeping to a thousand generations, connecting belief with fidelity that survives across generations while leaving cognacy unproven.

column5: Arabic ʾ-m-n / Hebrew ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary's root label for ءَامَنُوا۟ is Arabic ʾ-m-n; the psalm promises to tell God's אֱמוּנָה from generation to generation, joining faithfulness to the transmission of a spoken legacy.

column5: Arabic ʾ-m-n / Hebrew ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels ءَامَنُوا۟ with Arabic root ʾ-m-n and بِٱلْحَقّ with ḥ-q-q; Zechariah uses אֱמֶת from Hebrew root ʾ-m-n in a command to speak truth neighbor to neighbor, giving the faith/truth words a concrete communal setting while leaving cognacy unproven.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew ḥ-q-q; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels بِٱلْحَقّ as a right binding on heirs; Isaiah condemns חֹקְקֵי אָוֶן, those writing unjust statutes that deny the poor justice, showing that prescribed law can oppose the right the commentary describes.

The commentary calls the will binding, while the source lexicon's ʿ-ṣ-r (B006) gloss also evokes retracting a gift; Esther's sealed royal writing cannot be revoked, so redress requires a new counter-decree rather than withdrawal.
Proverbs warns that one who guarantees a stranger will suffer; beside the commentary's approving image of the guarantor standing behind another, it exposes the personal risk carried by that role.

Tobit tells his son, as his own death approaches, to bury him and not neglect his mother; this Jewish deathbed charge gives the commentary's image of a father's bequest to the living a concrete family setting.

The Mishnah opens with Moses receiving Torah and transmitting it through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the assembly; this Jewish tradition makes the commentary's successive handoff of counsel into an explicit chain of teachers.

The discussion of a sick person's oral gift asks when it takes effect and whether recovery permits retraction; it supplies a rabbinic legal lens on the commentary's binding testament and its source lexicon's contrasting image of a gift withdrawn.

In the closing testament scene, Job gathers his children and distributes his possessions, with a special inheritance for his daughters; this Jewish pseudepigraphic expansion makes the commentary's link between last counsel and heirs' shares unusually concrete.

A mother urges her youngest son not to fear execution but to accept death with his brothers; this Jewish martyr story makes counsel in faith under coercion a concrete analogue to the commentary's paired truth and ṣabr.

Jesus tells Peter that, once he turns back, he must strengthen his brothers; the instruction turns personal faith through a coming test into support passed to others, like the commentary's mutual counsel.
The writer tells Timothy to endure hardship and fulfill his ministry; read with the letter's imminent-death statement, it is a concrete last charge that carries steadfast service forward.
The writer says he is already being poured out and that the time of departure has come; this supplies an explicit deathbed frame for the succession and deposit language elsewhere in the letter.
The speaker says he knows that putting off his tent is imminent; like the commentary's dying testator, he frames his teaching as words left before death.
The speaker will ensure that his addressees can recall his teaching after his departure; this is a direct Christian formulation of advice preserved as a legacy.
Jesus is named guarantor of a better covenant; this supplies a distinct Christian use of surety for the commentary's figure who stands behind another's obligation.

column5: faith and endurance of the saints
column6: The verse identifies the saints by endurance, keeping God's commandments, and faith in Jesus; it brings faith and steadfastness together as a communal witness, though without the commentary's reciprocal advising.

The commentary's cited will procedure requires witnesses to swear, whereas James says not to swear and to let yes mean yes and no mean no; the contrast makes truthful speech without an oath an alternative account of reliable testimony.
Paul tells believers to bear one another's burdens; this gives a concrete communal form to the commentary's image of a guarantor standing behind another and carrying an obligation with them.

column5: law deposited beside ark as witness
column6: Moses tells Israel to place the written law beside the ark as a witness; this unites the commentary's inherited instruction, entrusted object, and witness in one testament-like act.
Jeremiah signs, seals, and has witnesses attest a purchase deed; the legal transfer gives the commentary's rights of heirs and witness scene a concrete documentary analogue.
The deed is placed in an earthen vessel so it may last many days; this closely matches the commentary's entrusted legacy preserved for successors.
Boaz calls the elders and people as witnesses that he has acquired Elimelech's property; this joins property succession to public testimony as the commentary does.
Jacob blesses each of his twelve sons according to his blessing; this is a distinct patriarchal testament in which the father's last words are distributed among successors.
Jacob grants Joseph one portion more than his brothers; this concretely develops the commentary's claim that an inheritance consists of apportioned shares.
The good person leaves an inheritance to children's children; this states directly the intergenerational transfer that the commentary uses to illuminate mutual counsel as a legacy.

column5: old age and testimony to generations
column6: The aging speaker asks to remain until he has told the coming generation of God's strength; this gives the commentary's deathbed image a living elder's explicit concern to pass testimony onward.
The psalm says its words are written for a generation yet to come; this makes the commentary's spoken bequest into a preserved written testimony for later believers.

column5: Jacob asks his sons about their faith
column6: The Talmud reads Jacob's deathbed gathering as his asking whether his sons remain faithful, to which they affirm Israel's God; this is a close Jewish interpretation of the commentary's Jacob asking what his sons will worship after him.
A man asks Jesus to tell his brother to divide the inheritance with him; this directly stages the claim over heirs' shares that the commentary treats as rights.

Jesus refuses the role of judge or divider in the inheritance dispute and warns against greed; this contrasts a legal allocation of heirs' rights with a warning that the claim itself can be spiritually misdirected.
In the rich fool parable, God asks who will receive the goods the man prepared after his death; this counters confidence in a self-managed estate with the uncertainty of who inherits it.
The Spirit is called the pledge of the believers' inheritance until its redemption; this closely joins the commentary's guarantor standing behind a claim with heirs awaiting their due.

Paul says he handed on what he first received about the Lord's Supper; this is a Christian formula for preserving a teaching and ritual across generations, matching the commentary's word passed from one believer to another.
The cup is identified with the new covenant and the rite is to be repeated in remembrance; this gives the commentary's transmitted counsel a specific liturgical form of communal remembrance.

Timothy is told to continue in what he learned and believed, knowing from whom he learned it; this explicitly links faith to a trustworthy chain of teachers, as the commentary links faith to counsel passed onward.

In the final charge before the writer speaks of his approaching death, Timothy is told to correct, rebuke, and exhort with complete patience and teaching; this directly pairs the commentary's mutual counsel with ṣabr.
The community is told to encourage one another and build one another up; this is a direct formulaic counterpart to the commentary's reciprocal act of enjoining one another.

column5: stirring one another to good works
column6: The readers are to consider how to provoke one another to love and good works; this directly joins reciprocal exhortation to the commentary's faithful people's good action.
The readers are told to keep assembling and encourage one another; this makes mutual counsel an ongoing communal practice rather than a solitary last instruction.
God confirms the promise to its heirs with an oath; this directly combines the commentary's heirs and sworn testimony, showing an oath used to assure rather than test a claimant.

column5: attempt to seize the heir's inheritance
column6: The tenants identify the owner's son as heir and kill him in hopes of taking his inheritance; this counter-scene makes the commentary's concern with heirs' rights vivid through their violent denial.
Moses publicly tells Joshua to be strong and lead the people into the land; this is a succession charge from a departing leader to the person who will carry the community forward.
Moses completes writing the law in a book before the farewell scene ends; together with its deposit by the ark, this makes the instruction a durable object for later generations.
Jacob declares Joseph's two sons to be his own sons for inheritance; this extends the commentary's discussion of who receives a share beyond the obvious line of sons.

Jacob predicts that the younger Ephraim will become greater than Manasseh, reversing birth order in a blessing; this complicates any reading of inherited portions as an unalterable firstborn entitlement.

Boaz explains that redeeming the property also preserves the dead man's name; this adds the continuation of a deceased person's household identity to the commentary's material inheritance and testament.
Jeremiah's witnessed deed is interpreted by the promise that houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in the land; this frames the preserved document as a promise to future inheritors.

column5: Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew ḥ-q-q; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels بِٱلْحَقّ with Arabic root ḥ-q-q and describes a binding right; the Hebrew king announces a חֹק, a decree, from the candidate root חקק, so the psalm shows a related legal sense without proving cognacy.
The royal son is promised the nations as his inheritance; this develops the commentary's image of a binding grant passing from a father to an heir.

column5: Arabic ʾ-m-n / Hebrew ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels ءَامَنُوا۟ with Arabic root ʾ-m-n; Deuteronomy joins Hebrew אֱמוּנָה, faithfulness, with God's justice and uprightness, bringing the commentary's adjacent faith and al-ḥaqq together while leaving the sound-based cognacy unverified.

column5: Arabic ʾ-m-n / Aramaic ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The commentary labels faith with Arabic root ʾ-m-n; Aramaic describes Daniel as מְהֵימַן, faithful, in a court where officials can find no fault except by attacking his observance of God's law, joining the root candidate to testimony and legal pressure.
The Mishnah defines the legal scope of an oath of testimony and the witnesses bound by it; it adds a rabbinic procedure for the compulsory witness oath that the commentary develops.

A midrash on Jacob gathering his sons reads the scene as his attempt to reveal the end of days, interrupted when the Divine Presence departs; this shifts the deathbed words from a family bequest toward an eschatological disclosure. Section numbering can vary by edition.
Believers are sealed with the promised Spirit after hearing and believing the message; this adds a seal of authentication to the commentary's pairing of entrusted faith and a guarantor.
Paul calls believers heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, provided they suffer with him; this links inheritance with endurance, a combination central to the commentary's reading of faith and ṣabr.
Jesus promises the land to the meek; this gives the commentary's patience and inheritance motifs an explicit Christian pairing, though in an eschatological rather than legal estate setting.

column5: farewell command to love one another
column6: Jesus gives his disciples a command to love one another on the eve of his death; this is a concrete last instruction entrusted to a community, though its content differs from the commentary's truth and patience.
Jesus says he leaves and gives his peace to the disciples; the farewell gift formula gives a distinct Christian example of a legacy passed to survivors.

Clement says the apostles appointed approved successors so that others could succeed them after their deaths; this early Christian account makes the commentary's chain of counsel an explicit succession of entrusted responsibility.

column5: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew ʿ-ṣ-r; package table's sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The Qur'anic word al-ʿaṣr is an oath by time, but the commentary separately reports a source-lexicon gloss under Arabic root ʿ-ṣ-r of giving and then withdrawing a gift; Genesis uses the Hebrew candidate root עָצַר for God closing wombs, a related withholding sense, not the verse's time oath. The sound correspondence is unverified.
